title: Fine-tuning (deep learning)
text:
In deep learning, fine-tuning is the process of adapting a computational model trained for one task (the upstream task) to perform a different, usually more specific, task (the downstream task).[1] It is considered a form of transfer learning, as it reuses knowledge learned from the original training objective.[2,3]

Fine-tuning involves applying additional training (e.g., on new data) to the parameters of a neural network that have been pre-trained.[4,5] Many variants exist. The additional training can be applied to the entire neural network, or to only a subset of its layers, in which case the layers that are not being fine-tuned are "frozen" (i.e., not changed during backpropagation).[6] A model may also be augmented with "adapters"—lightweight modules inserted into the model's architecture that nudge the embedding space for domain adaptation. These contain far fewer parameters than the original model and can be fine-tuned in a parameter-efficient way by tuning only their weights and leaving the rest of the model's weights frozen.[7]

For some architectures, such as convolutional neural networks, it is common to keep the earlier layers (those closest to the input layer) frozen, as they capture lower-level features, while later layers often discern high-level features that can be more related to the task that the model is trained on.[6,8]

Models that are pre-trained on large, general corpora are usually fine-tuned by reusing their parameters as a starting point and adding a task-specific layer trained from scratch.[9] Fine-tuning the full model is also common and often yields better results, but is more computationally expensive.[10]

Fine-tuning is typically accomplished via supervised learning, but there are also techniques to fine-tune a model using weak supervision.[11] Fine-tuning can be combined with a reinforcement learning from human feedback-based objective to produce language models such as ChatGPT (a fine-tuned version of GPT models) and Sparrow.[12,13]
